transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-13 11:00 AM PST | Duration: 55 mins | Recording: Fireflies
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alex Gomez (Redwood Solutions); Marcus Chen (HaloEdge CTO), Lena Ortiz (Platform), Samir Patel (SRE), Ivy Wu (Data)

Summary: Quick integration workshop to map HaloEdge inference path. Main asks: hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs for latency/cost, VPC/private deployment requirements, SDK/connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy pattern for multi-tenant quotas, and observability hooks for token-level cost and traceability.

Topics: integration kits, SDKs (python/node), LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway vs sidecar, rate limits and quotas per-tenant, observability/events/tracing, private deployment (VPC/on-prem), security and compliance (SOC2, KMS).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, that's Priya our systems engineer and Alex on solutions. How's it going Marcus?
[00:12] Marcus Chen: Hey Jordan, hey team thanks. We wanted to run through the integration surface and make sure we understand patterning — whether we go hosted, dedicated, or private and the impact on our gateway architecture.
[00:24] Jordan Lee: Great, that's exactly what we planned, was to map your flow. Priya you want to kick with a quick run of the runtime options?
[00:28] Priya Nair: Yeah sure. So at a high level Redwood offers hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployments into your VPC or on-prem. Hosted is fastest to start but has multitenant isolation; dedicated gives you predictable throughput and isolation and private is the full control option for regulated data.
[00:45] Lena Ortiz: Quick injection — when you say private, do we get a customer-managed control plane? We need no egress to your control plane for some workloads.
[00:52] Priya Nair: You can choose a private control plane where you manage the network. We also support an on-prem package if you need air-gapped. There are a few topology variants — VPC peering, PrivateLink style, or full air-gapped with local inference.
[01:05] Samir Patel: For our initial pilot we expected sub-150ms p95 for short prompts. Is that realistic on hosted or would we need dedicated?
[01:14] Priya Nair: Sub-150ms is tough on larger model configs. For smaller open models or quantized variants hosted can hit low latency, but dedicated tuned pools with proper batching and prewarmed KV cache are your best bet.
[01:26] Jordan Lee: Also worth noting we can route requests by policy; latency-sensitive routes can go to dedicated while lower-priority flows hit hosted to save costs.
[01:34] Marcus Chen: Routing by policy ok. How do we plug this into our gateway? We run an Envoy based gateway with an auth sidecar. We also use a request proxy for internal routing.
[01:44] Priya Nair: Two common patterns: 1) Edge gateway calls Redwood API directly with per-tenant API key and rate-limits enforced in your gateway; 2) You host a proxy/sidecar that handles authentication, local caching (prefix / KV cache), and fan-out to Redwood endpoints.
[01:58] Alex Gomez: The sidecar approach is popular when customers need tenant-level quotas and local metrics. The sidecar can implement constant-time tokenization, prefix caching, and local rate limiting to reduce calls.
[02:10] Lena Ortiz: Would that sidecar be open source or do we run Redwood's connector?
[02:14] Priya Nair: We provide an SDK and reference proxy. SDKs for Python and Node have native connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex. We also publish a reference gateway-connector repo that you can fork and run in your cluster. It's more of a template than an enforced component.
[02:29] Marcus Chen: On LangChain — we run ops with LangChain orchestration, and a bunch of our ingestion is LlamaIndex backed. How native are the adapters? Are they first-class or community maintained?
[02:40] Priya Nair: We maintain official LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters; they support streaming, function/tool calling, and structured outputs. There are a couple rough edges depending on the transformer model, e.g. kv cache handling in LlamaIndex when you use retrieval-augmented generation, but we have known patterns.
[02:58] Ivy Wu: You mentioned KV cache — can you explain how that works with long context windows? We have multi-document embeddings and we want to reuse token-level state across short summons.
[03:09] Priya Nair: Sure. The runtime manages per-request KV cache; for repeated prefixes we persist prefix caches and serve prefix hits which reduces token generation cost and latency. For long context you can do chunking plus retrieval and stitch on the client.
[03:21] Samir Patel: Does that require us to run a Redis or anything?
[03:24] Priya Nair: Not necessarily. The cache is server-side in Redwood for hosted/dedicated; with private/on-prem you can wire it to your cache store. The reference sidecar can optionally keep a local Redis for extreme low latency.
[03:35] Marcus Chen: Ok. Observability — we need token-level billing, per-route latency breakdowns, and request traces. Can you push traces into our X-Ray/Jaeger?
[03:46] Alex Gomez: Yes, the console gives per-route/model dashboards and token-level cost breakdown. For traces we support trace hooks and can emit events to a customer sidecar or push to an observability sink via OTLP. We also support log forwarding to your SIEM.
[04:01] Lena Ortiz: What about sample rate and PII scrubbing? We can't retain raw user content for more than 7 days and need scrubbing in the pipeline.
[04:10] Priya Nair: We have retention controls and field-level redaction options. For hosted we offer configurable retention windows; for private deployments you control retention fully. We can also recommend a scrubber in the reference connector.
[04:22] Marcus Chen: Security questions — do you support SAML SSO for the console and KMS integrations for keys?
[04:28] Jordan Lee: Yes to both. SSO via SAML/Okta, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations for model keys and audit logs are supported on dedicated and private tiers.
[04:38] Samir Patel: Competitors — we've looked at the usual suspects like openai for the API, but we are also evaluating vendor X that offers an on-prem runtime; how do you compare?
[04:47] Jordan Lee: A lot depends on ops overhead. Redwood's position is unified runtime + orchestration so you don't build the serving layer from scratch. We'll share a TCO comparison but the tradeoffs are build vs buy.
[04:56] Lena Ortiz: Let's talk quotas and rate-limits. We need per-customer daily token quotas and burst protection. How granular can Redwood get?
[05:05] Priya Nair: Very granular. We support per-token quotas, per-route and per-API-key rate limits, and you can configure burst windows. If you prefer the gateway to enforce quotas, you can push enforcement to the sidecar and use Redwood as a secondary layer.
[05:19] Marcus Chen: For multi-model routing — we plan to use smaller models for cheap generation and fall back to larger models for higher-quality responses. Can routing be automatic?
[05:29] Priya Nair: Yes, smart routing policies can route by latency, cost, or quality. You can set automatic fallback to a higher-capacity model or to a dedicated pool when hosted is saturated.
[05:40] Ivy Wu: Is model pinning per-tenant possible? We want to pin versions for A/B experiments.
[05:44] Alex Gomez: You can pin model versions per-route or per-customer. We also support canary rollouts and A/B experiments with automatic rollback on quality regressions.
[05:53] Marcus Chen: About the SDKs — do they support streaming responses into our web client? We use websockets and server-sent events.
[05:59] Priya Nair: Yes, SDKs support streaming and event-based delivery. We have examples for SSE and websockets in the repo.
[06:08] Jordan Lee: Wondering if we could sketch a minimal pilot — what would you like to validate in a 3-week pilot?
[06:15] Marcus Chen: Latency under load, per-tenant quotas, and LangChain adapter compatibility. Also security verification — SOC2 docs and KMS integration.
[06:24] Priya Nair: Sounds good. We usually propose a 2-3 week pilot using a dedicated dev pool, run a load generator that mimics your p95 target, and validate adapter flows with a small LangChain job set.
[06:34] Samir Patel: For load, we currently average 120 qps across tenants with peaks to 400 for short bursts. How do you recommend sizing?
[06:43] Priya Nair: We'll map QPS to tokens/s and model latency to estimate GPU qps; for burst we recommend a reserved baseline with a burst bucket configured. We'll share a sizing worksheet.
[06:53] Lena Ortiz: Network topology — we have a strict egress policy. Can inbound-only connections work for private?
[06:59] Alex Gomez: For private/on-prem we can do inbound-only depending on topology; full air-gapped is also possible with local inference packaging, but that requires more integration work.
[07:11] Marcus Chen: Any rough numbers on cost delta between hosted and dedicated? We expect dedicated to be higher but more predictable.
[07:17] Jordan Lee: Roughly dedicated has higher fixed cost but lower per-token cost at scale. Hosted is pay-as-you-go with higher variability. We'll send a modeled estimate based on your traffic.
[07:26] Ivy Wu: I noticed mention of quantization — do you support int8 or newer quant formats?
[07:31] Priya Nair: Yes, the runtime supports quantized variants and we recommend specific quant profiles per model. We'll give model-by-model guidance; some very large models behave differently so we test perf.
[07:42] Marcus Chen: On LlamaIndex specifically, we have an existing RAG pipeline. Any gotchas?
[07:48] Priya Nair: Two things: document chunking strategy and KV cache coordination. If you keep the tokenizer consistent and avoid double chunking, you'll see better latencies. We have a LlamaIndex recipe in our repo.
[07:59] Samir Patel: Observability again — how are errors surfaced? We need per-request error codes and sampling of payloads for debugging.
[08:06] Alex Gomez: Error taxonomy is surfaced in the console and via webhook; we can push a sampled payloads feed to your secure S3 for debugging.
[08:16] Marcus Chen: Great. Let's get into a tiny bit of code — Priya, could you show the Python SDK call pattern?
[08:21] Priya Nair: Sure. Example is simple: client = Redwood(api_key=..); resp = client.generate(model='rwd-small-v1', prompt='...') — it supports stream callbacks, tool/function calling, and output schema validation. For LangChain there's a wrapper LLM that plugs into the chain.
[08:36] Lena Ortiz: Any prebuilt connectors for our existing vector DB? We use a managed vector store for retrieval.
[08:40] Priya Nair: We have adapters for common vector stores; if you need a custom connector we can assist.
[08:46] Marcus Chen: One more on quotas — how are per-customer limits applied if we route some traffic via our gateway and some direct to Redwood?
[08:55] Priya Nair: You can choose to have the gateway enforce hard quotas. When calls go direct we recommend issuing short-lived per-tenant tokens scoped to their quota so enforcement is centralized.
[09:05] Samir Patel: Suppose we want to run benchmarks — what do you need from us to reproduce production-like load?
[09:11] Priya Nair: A representative prompt set, token distribution, session lengths, and concurrency profile. Also auth scaffolding for multi-tenant keys.
[09:19] Marcus Chen: We'll share those.
[09:21] Jordan Lee: Cool — let's do a rapid recap and assign owners.
[09:25] Marcus Chen: Recap: 3-week pilot on dedicated dev pool to validate latency and LangChain adapters; Redwood sends SOC2 and network docs; HaloEdge shares prompt set and traffic profile.
[09:36] Jordan Lee: That matches our notes. Action items: I'll send security + architecture docs; Priya will craft the benchmark plan; Marcus will provide traffic artifacts.
[09:45] Lena Ortiz: Timing — can we get the docs early next week? We're hoping to kick pilot in mid-March.
[09:51] Jordan Lee: We'll aim for that. We'll follow up with proposed pilot dates in the email.
[09:56] Samir Patel: One small concern: cost controls — we need per-tenant spend limits and alerts. Is that built into the console?
[10:03] Alex Gomez: Yes, billing alerts and per-API-key spend caps are supported. You can wire up webhooks for spend alerts.
[10:10] Marcus Chen: Okay thanks all. Any other questions before we wrap?
[10:13] Ivy Wu: Nothing from me.
[10:15] Lena Ortiz: No.
[10:16] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the doc bundle and scheduling options.
[10:20] Meeting end.
